title: Path traversal via unsanitized CSV column values used in file path construction in split_csv.
description: The split_csv method constructs output filenames by interpolating raw DataFrame column values into an f-string filename (f"{group_column}_{value}.csv"), then joins it with the output directory using pathlib's / operator. Column values originate from attacker-controlled CSV file content and are never sanitized for path-separator or directory-traversal characters. Pathlib does not prevent traversal sequences in the operand, so a value containing '../' resolves to a path outside the intended output directory.
impact: An attacker who supplies a malicious CSV file can write arbitrary files to any location writable by the process. This can overwrite configuration files, inject cron jobs, replace scripts, or plant web shells depending on the process's filesystem permissions.
attack_path: 1. Attacker crafts a CSV file where the group column contains a value such as '../../../tmp/evil' or '../../.bashrc'.
2. A user or automated pipeline calls handler.split_csv(df, group_column='category', output_dir='./split_files').
3. The method iterates df['category'].unique(), reaching the malicious value.
4. filename becomes 'category_../../tmp/evil.csv'.
5. filepath = Path('./split_files') / 'category_../../tmp/evil.csv' resolves to a path outside ./split_files/.
6. subset.to_csv(filepath, index=False) writes attacker-controlled data to the traversed path.
remediation: Sanitize the 'value' variable before using it in the filename by stripping or replacing path separators and traversal sequences. Apply os.path.basename() or replace '/', '\', and '..' characters. After constructing the full path, verify that the resolved path (filepath.resolve()) is still within the intended output_path.resolve() before writing. Example: filepath = output_path / re.sub(r'[^a-zA-Z0-9_.-]', '_', str(value)) + '.csv'; assert filepath.resolve().is_relative_to(output_path.resolve()).

title: XML entity expansion denial-of-service (Billion Laughs) via unprotected xml.etree.ElementTree parsing.
description: The ConstructionXMLReader class and all its subclasses (P6XMLReader, IFCXMLReader, COBieXMLReader, BSDDXMLReader) use Python's xml.etree.ElementTree.parse() and ET.fromstring() to parse XML data. Python's own documentation explicitly warns that 'The xml.etree.ElementTree module is not secure against maliciously constructed data.' These functions are vulnerable to exponential entity expansion (Billion Laughs) and quadratic blowup attacks, where a crafted XML document can expand to consume gigabytes of memory and CPU, causing denial of service.
impact: An attacker who supplies a malicious XML file (e.g., a crafted P6 schedule export, IFC-XML, or COBie-XML file) can cause the parsing process to consume all available memory and CPU, resulting in denial of service of the application or server.
attack_path: 1. Attacker creates an XML file with recursive entity definitions (Billion Laughs pattern): <!DOCTYPE lolz [<!ENTITY lol 'lol'><!ENTITY lol2 '&lol;&lol;&lol;...'>...]>.
2. The file is presented as a P6 schedule export, COBie file, or IFC-XML file.
3. User or pipeline calls reader.parse_file('malicious.xml') or reader.parse_string(malicious_xml_string).
4. ET.parse() or ET.fromstring() attempts to expand entities exponentially.
5. Memory and CPU consumption grow exponentially, crashing the process or starving the system.
remediation: Replace xml.etree.ElementTree with defusedxml.ElementTree (from the defusedxml package). Use defusedxml.ElementTree.parse() and defusedxml.ElementTree.fromstring() which disable entity expansion and DTD processing by default. Alternatively, use iterparse with a limited entity expansion count, or set a maximum file size check before parsing.

title: XML entity expansion denial-of-service in IDS specification parser via unprotected ET.parse().
description: The IDSValidator class in the BIM Validation Pipeline uses xml.etree.ElementTree.parse() to load IDS (Information Delivery Specification) XML files. This parser is vulnerable to the same XML entity expansion attacks (Billion Laughs, Quadratic Blowup) as the xml-reader skill. An attacker who can supply or tamper with an IDS specification file can cause denial of service through exponential memory consumption.
impact: An attacker who controls or modifies an IDS specification XML file can crash the BIM validation pipeline or the hosting server through exponential memory consumption, disrupting the automated validation workflow.
attack_path: 1. Attacker crafts a malicious IDS XML file with recursive entity definitions.
2. The file is provided as an IDS specification to the IDSValidator constructor: IDSValidator('malicious_ids.xml').
3. The _parse_ids method calls ET.parse(path) on the malicious file.
4. The XML parser attempts to expand entities exponentially.
5. The process consumes all available memory and crashes.
remediation: Replace xml.etree.ElementTree with defusedxml.ElementTree. Use defusedxml.ElementTree.parse() which disables entity expansion and DTD processing. Add a file size check before parsing to reject unreasonably large IDS files.

title: Mermaid diagram injection via unsanitized entity names enables graph manipulation and potential XSS.
description: The generate_lineage_graph method constructs Mermaid diagram syntax by interpolating entity names directly into graph node definitions using f-strings (e.g., f"    {node_id}[{name}]"). Entity names originate from register_entity calls which may include data from external systems (file names, table names, user-provided labels). Mermaid uses square brackets for node labels, so a name containing ']' closes the label prematurely and allows injection of arbitrary Mermaid syntax including edge definitions, additional nodes, or HTML content that some Mermaid renderers will execute.
impact: An attacker who controls entity names (e.g., via imported data source names or table names) can manipulate the visual lineage graph to hide malicious data transformations from audit review. In web contexts where Mermaid diagrams are rendered with HTML support, injected content could lead to cross-site scripting (XSS), enabling session hijacking or data exfiltration.
attack_path: 1. Attacker registers a data entity with a crafted name: tracker.register_entity(name=']-->|steal|attacker[Fake Source', source_id=src.id, entity_type='table').
2. A user calls tracker.generate_lineage_graph(entity_id) on a graph that includes the malicious entity.
3. The f-string f"    {node_id}[{name}]" produces a line like '    ENT_abc123[]-->|steal|attacker[Fake Source]'.
4. The Mermaid parser interprets this as a valid edge definition, altering the graph topology.
5. If rendered in a web application with HTML support in Mermaid labels, attacker-injected HTML/JavaScript executes in the user's browser.
remediation: Sanitize entity names before interpolation into Mermaid syntax by escaping or removing Mermaid control characters (], [, |, >, -, and backticks). Use Mermaid's quoted string syntax for labels where available, or replace all non-alphanumeric characters in names with underscores. Example: safe_name = re.sub(r'[\[\]|>\-`"<]', '_', name).
